claim: Impact comes from mostly conventional work with a small atypical tail. In Web of Science 1990-2000, papers high on both median conventionality and tail novelty are top-5% hits at 9.11 per 100 versus a 5 per 100 background; either one alone gives 5.3-5.8; neither gives 2.05.
agent_test: Build candidate sets as one conventional core plus one distant add-on versus all-distant versus all-conventional, at equal tokens. Score with blind judges and a hold-out check. Compare the hit rate of each mix.

claim: Reference-pair atypicality (Uzzi A) tracks expert 'new finding' judgments; the first-ever co-citation measure of Wang et al. mostly does not. Measure choice changes the answer.
agent_test: When scoring idea novelty inside the agent, never rely on one proxy. Use two (embedding distance to nearest prior items, and a judge rubric) and log disagreements.

claim: Atypicality and disruption measure different things. Across about 41M articles they correlate negatively in every discipline, period and team size. Atypical work extends known ideas into new topics; disruptive work replaces a dominant idea inside its own topic.
agent_test: Treat 'combine distant things' and 'replace the incumbent answer' as two separate operators with separate triggers. Test each alone and mixed on tasks where the correct answer overturns the default (ARC rule inversions) versus tasks that need a new frame.

claim: Mechanism for K03 (functional equivalence): displacement happens when the new idea does the same job as the incumbent but better; distant recombination joins complementary parts and rarely replaces anything. This is argued by the same group and has not been tested by an outside lab. Gap search: an outside group (Ustyuzhanin 2026) ties displacement to stance toward a named incumbent, and an independent embedding-cluster taxonomy (Huang 2026) separates cross-topic bridges from within-topic redirectors. Neither tests the functional-equivalence mechanism itself, so status stays single-source.
agent_test: For a task, ask the agent to name the incumbent answer and what job it does. Then require a candidate that does the same job within the same topic. Compare against a cross-domain candidate at equal tokens.

claim: Atypical papers are about twice as likely to be disruptive as conventional ones (61% vs 36%) in Lin, Evans and Wu 2022, yet the paper-level Pearson r between typicality and D is only -0.05, and the 2025 paper finds a negative A-D link. These two results from the same group look opposed and are not reconciled in the evidence. Gap search: the two papers differ on data (MAG vs OpenAlex), scope (1970 cohort vs all years), atypicality scale (z-score tail, 2.3% of papers, vs A-index continuous) and outcome (share disruptive vs mean D). They are not reconciled; a tail effect versus a bulk slope is a plausible but untested reading.
agent_test: None directly; resolve by reading both papers' definitions of 'highly atypical' (binned vs continuous, reference-based vs topic-based).

claim: The disruption index D (CD index) is unstable and construct-sensitive: it needs about 10 years to settle, depends on reference-list length, and gives implausible country rankings (Iraq 57.5%, Nigeria 56% positive D vs China 26.9%).
agent_test: Do not use D-like scores as a reward for the agent. Use only outcome-checked quality.

claim: The 'science is getting less disruptive' decline (Park et al.: CD5 down 91.9% to 100% across fields) is disputed. Holst et al. trace it to zero-reference records with CD=1 (97% of CD5=1 papers, 78% of patents), Petersen et al. to growing reference lists, Bentley et al. to unweighted counting, Macher et al. to patent truncation (88% of drop). Park et al. reply that the decline survives Holst's own data, and a 105-study review says most studies show decline.
agent_test: None for the agent. Relevant only as a warning that trend claims built on one citation index are fragile.

claim: The small-team disruption advantage (Wu et al. 2019) depends on citation window and reference-length handling. It flips sign at a 5-year window and reverses when reference counts are equalised (Huang and Xie: AUC 0.94-0.98 for a one-reference measure vs 0.26-0.79 for the standard index).
agent_test: None directly. Caution against 'small focused agent beats big committee' claims drawn from D.

claim: Risky research strategies pay more on average but not enough to cover the extra failure risk: mean citations 8.38 (repeat), 11.00 (new), 12.90 (jump); break-even needs new and jump moves to succeed 76% and 65% as often as repeat moves. Prize winners gamble more. Re-read in the gap search: repeat 85.8% vs new+jump 14.2% of statements, jumps 1.8%; break-even p(new)=0.76 and p(jump)=0.65 of p(repeat). No LLM equivalent found.
agent_test: Set a budget share for distant moves (for example 10-20% of candidates) and compare against 0% and 50% at equal tokens on a task with a verifier.

claim: Highly novel papers are riskier and pay off later: more top-1% hits in the long run, but a slow start, and a bias against them in short windows. Boundary: measure used was first-ever co-citation, which K02 says tracks expert judgment poorly. Gap search: Lin 2022 needs about ten years for disruption to settle; a five-year window cannot see a 2017 shift until 2022. No LLM test of an extra revision round.
agent_test: In the agent's selection, do not drop a distant candidate on early scores alone; give it one extra revision round before ranking.

claim: Unusual combinations of datasets bring about 15% more citations; once topic atypicality is controlled, only 1-4% remains. The combination effect is smaller than its raw size when topic is held fixed.
agent_test: Ablate: combine a distant source with the same topic frame versus a different frame; compare quality at equal tokens.

claim: Distant source-target analogies yield more original ideas for humans and for strong LLMs; weak LLMs benefit only when the source is far enough. LLMs transfer structure and function but not always surface features. Gap search detail: for o3 and Claude-Sonnet-4 the cross-domain effect is 0.02 over all pairs, 0.12 for the farther half, 0.24 for the farthest 10%; pooled LLMs need the closest 20% dropped. Originality rated by lay raters (split-half .81) trades off with feasibility at rho=-0.74. Human literature hints at an inverted U (not opened).
agent_test: Vary source distance (near, mid, far) in the cross-domain operator; measure judged originality and validity at equal tokens, per model strength.

claim: Cross-domain analogy retrieval lifts LLM solution diversity by 90-173% and the share of novel solutions from as low as 1.6-9.0% to 50.4-68.9% across Claude, GPT and Gemini on 50 research problems.
agent_test: Run the cross-domain retrieval step on and off on the same problem set; count distinct valid solutions and verifier pass rate at equal tokens.

claim: Retrieval and recombination pipelines (SciMON, Nova, Deep Ideation, combinatorial creativity framework, Scideator) raise novelty or diversity as scored by their own judges: Nova 3.4x unique novel ideas, Deep Ideation +10.67% over best baseline, Gu et al. +7-10% similarity to real later papers, Scideator creativity support 70.5 vs 61.0. Most use LLM or embedding judges that K17 says are unreliable; none ran the idea to a real outcome.
agent_test: Iterated outside-knowledge retrieval inside the generate step, with a verifier-based score, at equal tokens versus one-shot generation.

claim: Plain over-generation stops helping: of 4000 seed ideas per topic only about 200 (5%) are non-duplicates at cosine 0.8.
agent_test: Deduplicate candidates by embedding before scoring, and track unique-candidate count per token spent.

claim: Blind expert review rates LLM-agent ideas as more novel than expert human ideas (5.64 vs 4.84 on 1-10, 49 ideas per condition, 79 reviewers) and slightly less feasible. But after 43 experts spent 100+ hours executing ideas, AI ideas lost 1.05 (novelty), 1.76 (excitement), 1.88 (effectiveness) points while human ideas barely changed. Novelty after execution is no longer significantly different (4.93 vs 4.73, p=0.21). Gap search: outside NLP ideas, in code the novelty push cost correctness (GPT-4 pass@1 16.1% to 2.1% as technique bans accumulate, NeoGauge max 1.4); in math the share of novel correct answers rose with difficulty (55.39% to 83.01%) but novelty was LLM-judged.
agent_test: Never judge novelty from the idea text alone. Run the idea to a checkable result (code, proof, ARC grid) before keeping it, and compare idea-stage rank with outcome-stage rank at equal tokens.

claim: LLM judges cannot reliably judge novelty. Pairwise ranking accuracy is 45-53% vs 56.1% human-human; novelty classification macro-F1 is 12-17 for frontier models, with a medium-novelty bias and zero recall on 'not novel'; LLM judges prefer model-written research questions that experts reject (novelty mirage).
agent_test: Replace LLM novelty ratings with a checkable test (does it run, does it differ from nearest known solution by a measured distance) and compare against LLM-rated selection.

claim: Many LLM-generated research ideas hide copied work: experts found 24% of 50 documents were plagiarism (14% direct copy score 5, 10% score 4), verified by emailing authors, and automated checks missed it. Gap search: an embedding filter alone retrieved the known overlapping paper in the top 10 in 10.34% of 58 cases, versus 89.66% for facet-level re-ranking.
agent_test: Add a nearest-prior-work lookup to the agent's novelty claim step; count claims that collapse when the nearest source is shown.

claim: LLMs are individually about as original as people but collectively more alike: 22 LLMs had equal mean originality on three tests (AUT 0.711 vs 0.696) with significantly lower between-model variability. Humans with AI ideas write better individual stories but the set is more alike (10.7% lower diversity, search summary only). Gap search: NoveltyBench finds fewer than 3 distinct answers in 10 samples; Artificial Hivemind finds same-model similarity above 0.8 in 79% of cases and 71-82% across models.
agent_test: Measure within-agent sample diversity over N runs. Test forced distance (seed from a far source, or a different persona) versus temperature at equal tokens.

claim: AI use in science broadens individual output but narrows the shared field: about 3x papers and 4.8x citations, topic range -4.63%, engagement -22% (secondary summary, unopened). AI-assisted writing after 2023 goes with higher disruption but not broader sourcing (beta=0.151 at 18 months).
agent_test: None for the agent now; revisit if multiplayer sharing of findings is built, because shared agents may converge.

claim: Text-based novelty measures (embedding distance among cited titles, language-model surprisal, review-tuned classifiers) are valid against expert ratings only modestly: surprisal t=2.6 on 83 notes with 8 false alarms; SciBERT method-novelty accuracy 0.74; title-embedding scores correlate positively with self-reported newness.
agent_test: For the agent's novelty gate use a measured distance to nearest known items and calibrate it on a few labelled cases first.

claim: Disruption measures disagree with each other and with expert tags: the original index loaded negatively on a citation-impact factor, new-finding tags were negative in 45 Poisson regressions, and a zero-shot LLM rater was below chance (AUC 0.42) at spotting highly cited ICLR papers while an alternative measure scored 0.83.
agent_test: None; reinforces K06.

claim: Ideas for landmark papers often come from practical problems, talks and cross-field contact, not from the cited literature. Reference combinations are a trace of the work, not its cause.
agent_test: Compare generating from the problem statement alone versus problem plus cited-literature recombination on a verifiable task.

claim: Innovation has moved from foundation and extension toward generalization: top generalizing works reach 84.0% farther in reference space and are 114.0% more likely to get cross-domain citations. The disruption index mixes these three modes.
agent_test: Tag each operator output as foundation, extension or generalization and track which mode wins on verifier checks.

claim: Teams place atypical combinations inside conventional knowledge more than solo authors (37.7% more likely); team size is inverted-U for novelty in one survey-linked study; field variety correlates r=.25 with novelty.
agent_test: Multi-persona sampling (crowd within) versus single persona for the distant add-on; link to the Crowd within subfield.

claim: Forcing a code model away from known techniques costs correctness fast: on 199 Codeforces problems GPT-4 pass@1 falls 16.1, 11.6, 7.1, 5.2, 2.3, 2.1 (%) as technique bans accumulate while divergent creativity rises 4.5 to 15.3%. MCTS, self-correction, planning and sampling do not improve both.
agent_test: Put a distance budget on the cross-domain operator and gate each distant candidate with a unit test or checker; report pass rate by distance step.

claim: In competition math, more shown prior solutions raise correctness and cut novelty; harder problems lower correctness but raise the novel share of correct answers (55.39% to 83.01% from AMC 8 to the hardest sets). Novelty and correctness were judged by LLMs.
agent_test: Show the incumbent solution when displacing, but add an explicit differ-from-this instruction and check with a verifier, not an LLM judge.

claim: Prompt-level changes raise sample diversity without a measured quality loss: showing earlier answers and asking for a different one restores about human-level diversity (NoveltyBench, 20 models), and verbalizing k answers with probabilities raises diversity 1.6-2.1x and lifts downstream math accuracy 32.8 to 36.1-37.5 (Verbalized Sampling). Telling the model to be creative or paraphrasing barely helps.
agent_test: At equal tokens compare plain resampling, in-context regeneration, and verbalized-k generation by unique valid candidates per verifier call.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-27 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: No study tests the Uzzi mix with LLMs. Zhang et al. build generators from one conventional anchor and one distant cited paper but do not compare mix with all-distant or all-conventional sets. Random concept combinations double lexical diversity (0.41 vs 0.21) but cut relevance (0.05 vs 0.11).
agent_test: Three-arm test at equal tokens: all-conventional, all-distant, conventional core with one distant add-on; score with an executable verifier and a dedup count.

claim: Expert originality ratings are noisy: test-retest ICC 0.59-0.74 for overall quality and 0.60 for originality over two waves of 63 researchers; lay raters reach split-half 0.73-0.81. Originality trades off with feasibility at rho=-0.74. Reviewer scores are orthogonal to later disruptiveness (rho about 0.005) and an LLM rater scored AUC 0.42 for highly cited ICLR papers.
agent_test: Do not select candidates by an originality score alone; use a verifier first and treat originality as a tie-breaker.

claim: Displacement is tied to a named incumbent: a content signal for contesting or relying on the incumbent paradigm detects the RNN-to-Transformer shift in 2016-Q1, 25 quarters before a five-year disruption index could register the 2017 breakthrough.
agent_test: Make the agent state the incumbent answer and what job it does; count how often a candidate that contests it beats it on the verifier.

claim: No LLM budget-share study was found for distant moves. The human prior is: new and jump moves are 14.2% of published statements and need success rates of 76% and 65% of repeat moves to break even.
agent_test: Estimate the success ratio of distant versus near candidates with a verifier on a calibration set, then set the distant share from that ratio.
